Hello,

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
June 11, 2026

Metro Lakes Watershed District publishes 2025 Water Quality Report

The Metro Lakes Watershed District today released its 2025 Water Quality Report, covering monitoring at 10 sites across the district's three program phases. The report includes annual mean chloride, total phosphorus and water clarity results for each monitored lake, inlet and outlet.

Highlights:
- Chloride monitoring now covers 10 sites, including two Phase 3 stations added in 2025: the Lake Odegaard north inlet and the Penner Lake outlet.
- Annual mean chloride exceeded the state's chronic standard of 230 mg/L at four lake monitoring sites (Table 3).
- Chapter 2 summarizes winter salt use reported by member cities.

Chloride from road and parking-lot salt does not break down in water. Once it reaches a lake, it stays there until it is flushed out.

The full report is available at:

emails.subject: SEJ records webinar: what applies to the column
emails.content:
Hana,

I sat in on SEJ's records-request webinar at noon. Three things that apply to the column:

1. Under the Data Practices Act, an agency can't make us identify ourselves or say why we want public data.
2. Inspection is free. Copies of 100 pages or fewer top out at 25 cents a page. Past that, they can bill staff time, which is where estimates get padded. Ask for the estimate in writing first.
3. When a viral claim cites an agency, ask for the data file behind it, not the press release. If they keep it electronically, they have to give us an electronic copy when they reasonably can.

One question: if a request comes with a fee, can I put it on my card and bill it with the column, the way I do travel?

SEJ sent its sample letters this afternoon. I'll adapt the state one for Minnesota and send it over.

- Owen

emails.subject: Re: SEJ records webinar: what applies to the column
emails.content:
Owen,

Useful, thanks. Point 3 is how the column should work anyway.

Yes on fees. Put them on your card and bill them with the column they're for, same as travel. If an estimate comes back over $100, check with me before you pay it.

And yes, send the Minnesota letter when it's ready. I'd like a copy in the freelancer folder so other writers aren't starting from scratch.

emails.subject: Re: SEJ records webinar: what applies to the column
emails.content:
Hana,

Here it is, adapted from SEJ's state sample. Writers replace everything in parentheses. It asks for a written estimate before any work over $25, so we'll hear about costs well before your $100 line.

---

Date:
To: (responsible authority or data practices compliance official, by name if the agency's data access policy lists one)
(Agency name, mailing address or email)
Re: Request for public government data

This is a request under the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act, Minn. Stat. ch. 13, for copies of the following public government data:

(Describe the records: what they are, the office that keeps them, the date range. One subject per request.)

Please provide the data electronically, in the format in which they are maintained. For spreadsheets and databases, I request the native file or an export (.xlsx or .csv) rather than a PDF.

If there will be a charge, please send me a written estimate before doing any work that would cost more than $25. I understand that inspection of public data is free and that the agency may not charge for time spent separating public from not-public data.

If any data are withheld or redacted, please identify them and cite the specific statute or classification that applies, as Minn. Stat. 13.03 requires.

I'm glad to narrow this request if that would speed things up. Please call or email with any questions.

Thank you,
(Name)
(Outlet, or freelance)
(Phone and email)

---

My own copy has a few notes at the bottom for writers. The two that matter most: nobody has to say who they are or why they want public data, and there's no fixed deadline, so log the date sent and follow up at 10 business days.

- Owen

emails.content:
Hana,

The May column is in the CMS, rated Misleading.

The graphic traces back to a 2014 advocacy ranking built on EPA's Toxics Release Inventory. It sorts waterways by total pounds discharged under permit, so the biggest river with the most outfalls lands on top. It says nothing about concentration. The state's own assessments have the metro reach meeting most standards most of the time, with real trouble on sediment and nutrients, and that's where the column ends up.

Sources are listed at the bottom of the draft. I kept a PDF of the filed version for my files.

- Owen

emails.content:

2. Say how many waterways the ranking covered, so "number one" reads as a spot on a list, not a medal.

The rest is clean. If you can turn these by noon, it goes to copy desk this afternoon.

Thanks,
H.

emails.subject: Re: May fact-check filed: Mississippi 'dirtiest river'

emails.subject: July fact-check filed: wetlands 'since 2000'
emails.content:
Hana,

July is in the CMS, rated False, with the historic loss up top as you asked.

Minnesota has lost roughly half of its original wetlands, but nearly all of that happened between settlement and the 1980s, mostly to farm drainage. The DNR's status and trends monitoring, which started in 2006, shows net change of a fraction of a percent per cycle, some cycles up and some down. The viral post took the long-run figure and pinned it on the last 25 years.

The source list is at the bottom of the draft.

- Owen

Could you add a sentence near the end about what the state still loses each year to development and drainage, even if the net number is small? One sentence should do it.

Thanks,
H.

emails.subject: Re: July fact-check filed: wetlands 'since 2000'
emails.content:
